title: Nanquan's cat
hook: a hard koan: monks quarrel over a cat; Zhaozhou puts his sandals on his head (Gateless Gate 14)
tomorrow: Every day is a good day

segments.voice: Yesterday: original face, and your line, before you were born. Today's koan is a hard one.

A quarrel, a cat, a sharp blade, and then, strangely, a pair of straw sandals worn as a hat. It's the fourteenth case of the Gateless Gate. Every tradition has stories its own people argue about: stories that don't sit right, that get skipped in the nice version, that make a thoughtful reader put the book down for a minute. Zen has several, and this is one of them. Fair warning: an animal dies in this story. i'll tell it plainly, say what Buddhists themselves say about it, and not pretend it's comfortable.
screen: `A QUARREL AND A CAT.` → `SANDALS WORN AS A HAT.` → `STORIES THAT DON'T SIT RIGHT.`

segments.voice: At Nanquan's monastery, the monks of the eastern hall and the western hall were quarreling over a cat. Who it belonged to, the story doesn't say. Nanquan picked the cat up and held it out. He said: if any of you can say a true word, I'll spare the cat. If not, I'll cut it. No one could answer. Nanquan cut the cat in two. That evening Zhaozhou, Nanquan's student, the one from mu and the washed bowl, came back from a trip. Nanquan told him what had happened. Zhaozhou took off his straw sandals, put them on his head, and walked out. Nanquan said: if you had been there, the cat would have been saved. So what do Buddhists do with this? The first precept is not to take life, and the story seems to break it. Teachers answer in different ways. Some say it probably never happened, a teaching story meant to shock, like Juzhi's finger. Some say Nanquan took the harm on himself to cut through the monks' quarrel. Some modern teachers say plainly that the story troubles them and that no teaching justifies killing. Those who keep the koan say it asks something real. The monks were so caught in owning and arguing that when life itself was on the line, they froze. Zhaozhou's sandals on the head seem to say: you had it upside down. The quarrel was on top and the cat was underfoot. Nobody has one agreed answer. That's why it's called hard.
screen: `EAST HALL AGAINST WEST HALL.` · `SAY A TRUE WORD, OR THE CAT.` · `THE PRECEPT AND THE STORY.` · `THE QUARREL UPSIDE DOWN.` · then, large: `SANDALS ON THE HEAD.`

segments.voice: Let this story, or another story that disturbs you, sit in the room with you, without rushing to fix it, excuse it or throw it out. Notice what it does in the body, a tight jaw, a turned stomach, and breathe with that. You might ask quietly what a true word would have been; if no answer comes, let that be all right, since some stories are carried, not solved.
Nanquan's cat. Monks quarreled over a cat and couldn't say a true word; hearing of it, Zhaozhou put his sandals on his head.
Your line: sandals on the head. A hard story, held honestly. Day two hundred eighty-five.

what a scholar hears: the case also appears in the Blue Cliff Record (cases 63–64) and the Book of Serenity, and modern teachers have debated whether it should be read literally at all.
